From the garden diary

pages.title: Our Studio
pages.content:
Botanica is a small studio at the end of a long garden. We grow most of what we sell in raised beds and two old greenhouses, and arrange it at a scrubbed oak table that has seen more flowers than we can count.

We started with a market stall and a van. The stall became a shop, the shop grew a garden, and the garden slowly took over the car park. Customers tell us they come for the flowers and stay for the conversation, which suits us fine.

What we believe

  • Flowers should be in season, local and free of plastic wrap.
  • A garden for cutting can still be a garden for bees.
  • Anyone can learn to arrange flowers; it just takes a few good ones and permission to experiment.

pages.title: Workshops
pages.content:
Our workshops run on Saturday mornings from spring to late autumn. Each one is two hours long, limited to eight people, and includes every flower, tool and slice of cake.

This season

  • Hand-tied bouquets: the spiral technique, step by step.
  • Table arrangements: low, loose and long-lasting, without floral foam.
  • Dried flower wreaths: for autumn and well into winter.
  • Houseplant clinic: bring a sad plant, take home a plan.

To book, call in at the shop or write to studio@example.com. Gift vouchers are available for every workshop.

posts.title: Delphiniums: the blue everyone asks about
posts.content:
Every June someone stops at the gate and asks what the tall blue flowers are. They are delphiniums, and they are worth the small amount of fuss they need.

Growing them

  • Full sun and rich, well-drained soil.
  • Stake them early, before the first summer storm, not after.
  • Slugs love young shoots; protect them in spring.
  • Cut the first spikes as they fade and you will often get a second, shorter flush in late summer.

In the vase

Cut when about a third of the flowers on the spike are open, and put them straight into deep, cool water. They drop their petals when they are done, all at once, which is either sad or rather beautiful depending on your mood.

comments.author: Margaret
comments.content: Mine flopped over in the first rain last year. Staking this year, early, as instructed!

posts.title: Bellflowers for shady corners
posts.content:
Every garden has one: the strip along the north fence where nothing seems to grow. Ours used to be bare earth and a hose reel. Now it is full of bellflowers.

Campanulas cope with part shade better than most flowering perennials, and the Cornish bellflower in particular will spread into a loose, white-flowered carpet that bees adore.

Plant for the place you have, not the place you wish you had.

Give them a mulch of leaf mould in autumn, cut them back after the first flowering, and they will ask very little else.

posts.title: Why we leave the thistles
posts.content:
Visitors are sometimes surprised to find thistles in a flower garden. We leave a few on purpose.

On a warm afternoon a single thistle head can have three or four kinds of bee on it at once. Later the seed heads feed goldfinches, and the down lines more than one nest.

We keep them to one corner, cut most heads before they seed, and wear gloves. That is all it takes to share the garden with the insects that pollinate everything else in it.

posts.title: Anthuriums indoors: light, water, patience
posts.content:
Anthuriums are the glossy, heart-shaped flowers that last for weeks. In the wild they grow in the warm, damp shade of the forest, and indoors they want something similar.

  1. Light: bright but indirect. A metre from a sunny window is ideal.
  2. Water: when the top few centimetres of compost are dry, not before.
  3. Humidity: a bathroom with a window is anthurium heaven.
  4. Patience: a new plant often sulks for a month while it settles in.

If the leaves yellow, it is usually too much water. If the flowers stop, it is usually too little light.

posts.title: The sunflower wall, week by week
posts.content:
In April we sowed a single row of sunflowers along the back wall. By August they were taller than the wall.

  • Week 1: seed in, netting over to keep the birds off.
  • Week 4: thinned to one plant every 30 centimetres.
  • Week 10: first buds, and the first visitors asking about them.
  • Week 16: in full flower, facing east every morning.

For cutting, choose the branching varieties: one plant gives a dozen smaller flowers over the summer instead of a single giant head.

posts.title: Desert lessons from a single saguaro
posts.content:
A saguaro may take ten years to grow its first few centimetres and seventy before it grows an arm. It is a good plant to think about when you are tempted to water a cactus on the windowsill every week.

Desert plants store water and grow slowly. Indoors that means a gritty compost, a pot with a drainage hole, the sunniest spot you have, and water only when the compost is completely dry, which in winter can mean once a month.

Most cacti that die indoors are loved to death.

posts.title: Hibiscus that last more than a day
posts.content:
Each hibiscus flower opens for a day or two and then it is done. The trick to a plant that is always in flower is not a longer-lasting bloom, it is more buds.

Feed every two weeks in summer with a high-potash feed, keep the plant in the brightest spot you have, and do not move it once it has buds: hibiscus drops them at the slightest change.
